paper_metadata.title: Quantum Monte Carlo for Economics: Stress Testing and Macroeconomic Deep Learning

summary: This paper studies quantum Monte Carlo for economics using simulator-based amplitude estimation benchmarks, not hardware runs. It reports a toy Gaussian integral with m=5 discretization qubits and n=6 phase-estimation qubits, a two-bank/two-period stress test with 10 estimation qubits yielding 1.622% versus a 1.618% theoretical loss, and a simplified DSGE benchmark with fitted error scaling of about N^-0.642 (approximate R) and N^-0.996 (exact R).

experiments.description: Quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) simulation of a simple Gaussian expectation value with a trigonometric payoff, used as a toy benchmark for amplitude estimation and circuit decomposition.

algorithm.variant: Quantum Monte Carlo with phase estimation (Brassard et al.)

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Probability distribution p(x) encoded on m=5 qubits; payoff f(x)=sin^2(x) encoded on an ancilla qubit; phase estimation register of n=6 qubits used for amplitude estimation.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Estimate mu = E[f(x)] = ∫ p(x) f(x) dx for p(x)=N(0,1), f(x)=sin^2(x).

problem_instance.description: Toy Monte Carlo integration problem for a Gaussian random variable and trigonometric payoff.

dataset_specification.description: Discretized Gaussian on 32 grid points over [-pi, pi].

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Discretize continuous x into M=32 points; normalize p(i)=p(x_i)/sum_i p(x_i).
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: PennyLane simulation; output phase distribution shown in Figure 5; analytical expectation used as reference.

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Discretization of the Gaussian distribution and normalization of probabilities.
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Estimate theta from measured bitstrings and convert to mu via mu=(1-cos(pi*theta))/2.

speedup_claims.conditions: amplitude estimation with phase estimation; idealized oracle model
speedup_claims.caveats: No wall-clock benchmark for this toy example; speedup is in oracle/query complexity.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: O(1/epsilon) oracle applications for amplitude estimation
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: O(1/epsilon^2) samples for classical Monte Carlo

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: Not assessed; toy benchmark with m=5 discretization qubits and n=6 phase-estimation qubits.
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Requires efficient state preparation for a Gaussian distribution, ancilla encoding of sin^2(x), and phase estimation; no hardware execution reported.

notes: num_qubits inferred as 12 from m=5 discretization qubits + 1 ancilla + n=6 phase-estimation qubits.
hardware.type inferred as simulator_other because the paper states the circuit is simulated in PennyLane and no real QPU is used.
The paper reports only a noiseless simulator demonstration in PennyLane and compares scaling analytically to classical Monte Carlo.

experiments.description: QMC stress-testing application: estimate expected capital losses of a two-bank system over two stress periods with Beta-distributed default shocks.

algorithm.variant: Quantum Monte Carlo with phase estimation for stress-testing

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Each default-rate variable d_t discretized into M=2^m points with m qubits per period; probability distribution encoded by A; payoff encoded by arithmetic circuit R and ancilla rotation.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Estimate expected system-wide capital loss fraction E0[loss_T%] for the two-bank, two-period stress scenario; after substitution the target becomes expectation of 0.0064*(2+d2)*(1+d1).

problem_instance.description: Stylized macroprudential bank stress test with credit losses and fire sales for two banks over two periods.

dataset_specification.description: Two-bank calibration in Table 1; default shocks d_t ~ Beta(2,10).

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Scenario parameters substituted into closed-form loss expression; default-rate variables discretized and encoded into quantum registers.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Compare QMC estimate to theoretical value; report fractional error for 2 and 10 estimation qubits; Figure 8 shows error vs oracle applications.

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Closed-form derivation of loss expression and parameter substitution from the stress-test calibration table.
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Convert estimated theta to expected loss; compare against theoretical loss 1.618%.

convergence_data.loss_curve_shape: error decreases with oracle applications until discretization error dominates

speedup_claims.conditions: QMC amplitude estimation on the two-bank, two-period stress test
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper reports simulation results in PennyLane; no real hardware run. Discretization error begins to dominate for N > 10^6.

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: Not assessed; the paper reports 10 phase-estimation qubits and a 2-period, 2-bank toy stress-test instance.
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Requires quantum arithmetic for the loss function, distribution loading for Beta(2,10), and phase estimation; no hardware benchmark is reported.
limiting_factors: Discretization error dominates at large N

notes: The paper does not state a single total qubit count for the stress-test circuit; only the structure (T periods, m qubits per variable, ancilla, and phase-estimation register) is described, so num_qubits is left null.
Circuit depth is not explicitly reported for the stress-test experiment; only qualitative gate-count/resource discussion is given.
The paper reports a simulator result of 1.622% versus a theoretical 1.618% loss, with fractional error 0.0027 at 10 estimation qubits and 0.023 at 2 estimation qubits.

experiments.description: QMC benchmark for a simplified neoclassical DSGE investment model, comparing exact and approximate encodings of the random-variable unitary and measuring error scaling versus oracle calls and wall-clock time.

algorithm.variant: Quantum Monte Carlo for neoclassical investment model; exact F and linear-approximation F
algorithm.parameter_initialization: Variational circuit for A trained with gradient descent; initial parameters not specified.

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Probability distribution of z' encoded on m=5 qubits; linear random variable encoded on ancilla via controlled-Y cascade; phase estimation register of n qubits used for amplitude estimation.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Estimate expectation of a linearized Bellman-error-related random variable for the simplified neoclassical model, derived from loss |(1/Ns) sum_j (C1 + C2 z'_j)|.

problem_instance.description: Simplified neoclassical stochastic investment model used as a macroeconomic deep-learning benchmark.

dataset_specification.description: Normal shock z' with mean 1 and sigma 0.02; constants C1=30, C2=-29 chosen near optimal values.

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Discretize z' on 32 points over [0.94,1.06]; train a variational circuit to approximate the target distribution; linearize the random-variable encoding.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Error epsilon vs number of oracle applications N; compare exact F and approximate F; log-log linear fits reported in Figure 9.

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Train a 10-layer variational circuit to approximate the discretized normal distribution; discretize z' and rescale the payoff to fit the amplitude-estimation encoding.
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Convert estimated theta to expectation value mu; fit error scaling in log-log space.

convergence_data.loss_curve_shape: training cost decreases over 3000 epochs; quantum estimation error scales approximately as N^-0.996 (exact) and N^-0.642 (approximate)

speedup_claims.caveats: Exact scaling is shown in simulation; practical runtime depends on gate times and hardware noise.
Approximate implementation degrades scaling from -1 to about -2/3.
This is a projected wall-clock comparison based on assumed gate times, not a hardware experiment.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: O(1/epsilon) for exact F; approximately O(epsilon^-3/2) for linear approximation of R
complexity_analysis.wall_clock_quantum: 1 ns gate time can outperform a strong HPC cluster at error 1e-8 by 5.6x
complexity_analysis.wall_clock_classical: Strong HPC cluster and supercomputer baselines extrapolated from classical Monte Carlo timing

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: Not assessed; benchmark uses m=5 discretization qubits and n in [3,7] for the plotted scaling, with no hardware run.
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Requires variational state preparation for A, approximate or exact R encoding, and phase estimation; the paper only extrapolates runtime from gate depth.
limiting_factors: Large gate depth from amplitude estimation
Approximate R reduces scaling to about N^{-2/3}
Classical HPC remains faster in the reported benchmark

notes: The paper reports m=5 discretization qubits and a range of phase-estimation qubits n=3..7, but does not give a single total qubit count for the benchmark; total qubits depend on n and ancilla/register overhead.
Circuit depth is discussed via gate counts and depth plots (Figure 13) but no single numeric depth is stated in the text for this experiment.
The paper reports fitted scaling exponents of about -0.642 for the approximate R implementation and -0.996 for the exact case, but only on simulation and extrapolated runtime.

experiments.description: QMC benchmark for a more realistic consumption-saving DSGE model with multiple exogenous shocks, demonstrating quadratic scaling of estimation error with respect to oracle calls for two- and three-random-variable cases.

algorithm.variant: Quantum Monte Carlo for consumption-saving model with occasionally binding borrowing constraint

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Multiple exogenous variables encoded into separate registers; QMC used to estimate MSE of Bellman error in the deep-learning solver.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Estimate the Bellman-error MSE in the deep-learning solution of the consumption-saving model.
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Borrowing constraint ct <= wt handled in the underlying economic model; no quantum-specific constraint handling reported.

problem_instance.description: Consumption-saving problem with exogenous stochastic shocks and an occasionally binding borrowing constraint.

dataset_specification.description: AR(1) shock processes for income, interest rate, and discount factor; Gaussian innovations.

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Classical deep-learning solver samples endogenous and exogenous variables; QMC replaces Monte Carlo averaging in the Bellman-error estimate.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Figures 11 and 12 report scaling exponents for two- and three-random-variable cases; Table 2 reports classical training time and final error for varying MC draw counts.

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Sample endogenous and exogenous variables; evaluate Bellman error with a neural network.
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Fit scaling exponents of error vs oracle calls for the QMC runs.

convergence_data.loss_curve_shape: Bellman error decreases with more random draws; QMC scaling exponents reported as -1.0283 (two variables) and -0.9557 (three variables)

classical_baselines.method_name: classical deep learning with monte carlo sampling
classical deep learning with monte carlo sampling

speedup_claims.baseline_method: classical monte carlo sampling in deep learning
speedup_claims.conditions: multivariate QMC estimation for Bellman-error MSE
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper reports simulated scaling exponents for 2- and 3-variable cases; no wall-clock benchmark for this multivariate case.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: Quadratic speedup in oracle calls for multivariate Monte Carlo estimation
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: Classical Monte Carlo scaling in the deep-learning loss estimate

notes: The paper reports that the circuit was simulated on a classical computer and that the number of discretization qubits had to be reduced from 5 to 3 per variable to make the simulation feasible, but it does not provide a single total qubit count for the multivariate cases.
No explicit circuit depth is given for the multivariate consumption-saving benchmark.

experiments.description: Time-based benchmark comparing QMC and classical Monte Carlo for the simplified neoclassical model, using gate counts and assumed gate times to estimate wall-clock crossover against HPC cluster and supercomputer baselines.

algorithm.variant: QMC runtime benchmark with approximate R unitary

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Same neoclassical-model encoding as exp_3; runtime benchmark uses the approximate linear R unitary and the same discretized distribution.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Compare wall-clock time to reach a target estimation error for QMC versus classical Monte Carlo.

problem_instance.description: Runtime comparison for the simplified neoclassical macroeconomic deep-learning problem.
problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Use gate counts and circuit depth from the approximate QMC implementation; extrapolate classical Monte Carlo timing from sampled runs.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Figure 14 and Figure 15 compare extrapolated error-vs-time curves for QMC and classical Monte Carlo under different gate times.

implementation_details.classical_solver: Classical Monte Carlo and HPC extrapolation baselines
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Fit classical Monte Carlo error and runtime in log-log space; define cluster and supercomputer speedup baselines.
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Convert circuit depth to runtime via assumed gate time t; compare against classical extrapolations.

convergence_data.loss_curve_shape: Error decreases with runtime; QMC line slope steeper than classical, with crossover depending on gate time

speedup_claims.caveats: Projected from circuit depth and assumed gate times; not a physical hardware benchmark.

speedup_claims.factor: QMC can outperform strong computational clusters for gate times below 10 ns
speedup_claims.caveats: Crossover depends on gate time and target error.

speedup_claims.factor: supercomputer crossover for gate times faster than 10 ns in the ideal-scaling hypothetical
speedup_claims.conditions: hypothetical ideal scaling exponent -1 with same depth
speedup_claims.caveats: This is explicitly hypothetical and not the measured approximate implementation.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: Approximate QMC scales as O(epsilon^-3/2) in the linear-R implementation; ideal QMC would scale as O(1/epsilon)
complexity_analysis.constant_factor_quantum: Depends on gate time; 1 ns gate time yields 5.6x speedup over strong HPC cluster at epsilon=1e-8
complexity_analysis.constant_factor_classical: Strong HPC cluster = 1000x CPU; supercomputer = 1000000x CPU
complexity_analysis.crossover_n: Gate times below 10 ns can outperform a strong HPC cluster; 1 ns gate time crosses at error 1e-8 with 5.6x speedup
complexity_analysis.wall_clock_quantum: Derived from circuit depth times assumed gate time
complexity_analysis.wall_clock_classical: Derived from classical Monte Carlo timing extrapolation
